6.0.s.en: (1) The miracle of feeding the multitudes

6.0.0.en: "After these things": that is, after what happened in Jerusalem, the Lord headed to Galilee, and crossed its sea from west to east.

6.0.1.en: "Tiberias": a city on the Sea of Galilee, built by Herod and named after the Roman emperor "Tiberius" in the year 26 AD.

6.0.2.en: The crowds followed the Lord Jesus because of the many miracles of healing, so He went up to a high hill with the Twelve, and the crowds began to increase around Him.

6.1.0.en: This incidental remark which St. John mentioned, that the Passover was near, cannot be overlooked, for the discussion in this chapter will deal with the bodily feeding of the crowds on the one hand, and the spiritual, saving feeding of the whole world through the bread of life, the body of Christ, on the other. St. John referred to the Passover deliberately, to prepare the mind to link the body of Christ offered to the world with the saving Passover, "for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Cor 5:7).

6.2.0.en: Philip represents the rationalist character, for it was Christ who went to him to call him, and he did not follow Him of himself (ch. 1:43), and he is the one who interrupted Christ in His discourse: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us" (ch. 14:8).

6.2.1.en: For this reason, Christ directed the question to him in particular, to test his faith on the one hand, and to make him a witness that faith surpasses reason and material and mental resources. And because Philip represents the limited mind in its solutions, he did not offer a solution to the Lord Jesus' question about where to buy bread, but added another complication, namely how much?! ... that is, even if the place were available, where is the money?

6.2.2.en: The mind, in many cases, is an obstacle that limits God's work in our lives by its limited calculations ... So never let your mind be an obstacle to the life of faith, but make it receptive, thankful for God's works in your life, remembering them and meditating on them.

6.3.0.en: "A lad ... barley": St. John draws our attention to something important, which is that God works with the little, so the solution to the problem came through a small boy, and not one of the rich officials. Likewise the barley is the bread of the poor common people, not like wheat, the food of the rich.

6.3.1.en: Therefore, we must not despise the smallest things, nor boast of the greatest, but boast in the Lord, who with the least of the little does the most of the much. Would that we had this faith, active and working, in offering our weak resources to God, so that He does much with them.

6.4.0.en: "Make the men sit down": an organizing action, arranged by the disciples. For this reason it was easy to count the number of the men, and also easy to distribute; order is one of the Christian virtues of conduct to which God alerts us: "Let all things be done decently and in order" (1 Cor 14:40).

6.4.1.en: However, the total number was greater than this, as St. Matthew indicated: "beside women and children" (Mt 14:21).

6.4.2.en: We note that the phrase "as much as they would" points to the perfection of the divine work in satisfying them to overflowing. So God always acts toward every creature, and especially His children who rely on Him, for "the blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and He addeth no sorrow with it" (Prov 10:22).

6.5.0.en: Gathering the fragments ... that nothing be lost:

6.5.1.en: First, the direct meaning: the Lord wanted to make this miracle a memorial that the disciples would not forget, so the number of baskets matched their number, and each one of them carried one as a witness he would not forget, because he had shared in it.

6.5.2.en: The Lord also wanted to teach us to be prudent in our consumption of food, so that we keep what is left over to come back and eat it, and do not fall into the sin of extravagance, or of making light of the blessings of God which He has given us.

6.5.3.en: Second: the symbolic meaning in gathering the fragments is that this bread is a sign of His body. First He gave thanks, blessed, and distributed; these are the same steps He took when He instituted the sacrament of the Eucharist (thanksgiving). For this reason it was not acceptable for the fragments of bread to be left to be trodden by feet. Rather He asked the disciples, who represent the priesthood of the New Testament, to gather the remains of what symbolizes His body which He blessed and distributed.

6.5.4.en: Note, beloved, that in the rite of the Coptic Liturgy nothing of the body of Christ is left over, but the priest does what the disciples did in gathering all the remains of the body of the Lord, and leaving nothing of it ...

6.5.5.en: May we learn from Christ to pray before we eat our food, and to thank Him, and to bless it by making the sign of the Cross, then distribute the food to those present. And after we finish eating, we gather what is left to eat it, or give it to the needy, for this makes us feel the grace of God that He gives us and that many do not find.

6.6.0.en: The reaction of the souls to the miracle was limited, for they regarded Christ as the prophet of whom Moses spoke in (Deut 18:15-18), and their minds turned to installing Christ as an earthly king over them, which the Lord did not accept from them, so He departed alone, rejecting the glory of the world for which He had not come.

6.6.1.en: My beloved God ... make Your body my true satisfaction, and make my weakness and limited resources into strength, for I am less than a loaf of barley, but in Your hand I long to be a source of satisfaction for others, to speak to them about You, and call them to You so that they come to Your Church and have true satisfaction in place of the falseness and emptiness of the world.

6.7.s.en: (2) The miracle of walking on the water

6.7.0.en: On the same day as the feeding of the crowds, at its evening, the disciples, without the Lord, took a boat to cross the Sea of Galilee to Capernaum.

6.7.1.en: Let us note the expressions which St. John gives with precision (the darkness, Jesus was not [there], the sea arose). It is as though the Evangelist is painting a picture with great precision, for he says that the moments of true weakness (the darkness) in a man's life are the disappearance of Christ from his life, which lets Satan and trials (the great wind) buffet this man, so that his soul is tormented and he falls prey to fear instead of reassurance and safety. And when weariness exhausted them, from the struggle and effort they were in, rowing about 3 or 4 miles, that is, when man runs out of every device and every effort, Christ comes declaring Himself with power, "It is I; be not afraid" ... and peace takes the place of anxiety, and calm the place of tension, as the soul rests in its Savior.

6.7.2.en: My beloved God ... never leave me, and do not let me, through folly, leave You, for the winds are harsh and the storm is overwhelming, and I have no rescue except Your calm, strong voice: "It is I; be not afraid"; make these words a support for me throughout my life, and let me always pray with Your Church: "O King of peace ... give us Your peace."

6.7.3.en: Note: the Arabic translation, "they were willing to receive Him," is a very weak translation. In the Greek and English it came with the meaning of "they gladly received Him," which is stronger in meaning and depiction, and an expression of the state the disciples were in when they knew His voice.

6.8.0.en: In these three verses is the announcement of the miracle, and its perception by the crowds, for they knew that Christ had been at Galilee alone, and that the disciples had taken the only boat. How then did Jesus reach them? They had been standing waiting for Him to come from the mountain, and behold, He was with His disciples in Capernaum. For this reason the crowds also went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

6.9.s.en: (3) The food that perisheth and the food that endureth

6.9.0.en: The Jews, seeking Jesus, begin with a question of wonder about how He reached Capernaum. But Christ answers them as One who knows their inner selves: they seek Him not because of faith in the miracles He did, but only for the material gift, which is free food and satisfaction without toil, so they deserved Christ's rebuke of them, and His counsel to them that there is another kind of food that these do not know, and that none gives except Christ to everyone who follows Him, and it is spiritual food offered as a pledge of eternal life. The discourse here is an introduction to what Christ will take us to in the rest of the chapter, that He Himself is the living spiritual food. As for the expression "Him hath God the Father sealed," it refers to Christ and not the food, for Christ is the One appointed from eternity by the Father to give eternal life. And the Father bore witness to Him from His baptism with an audible voice, and this witness was like a declaration and seal, that is, a confirmation by the Father of the Son's work.

6.9.1.en: My beloved God ... I still find in myself a concern for the food that perisheth, so I seek material goods and earthly success, forgetting that all this is passing away. Lift my heart, my God, to what is above, so that I seek You, and all my longings become spiritual, centered on You, O food that endureth, O bread of life.

6.10.0.en: The Lord Christ said in (v. 27): "Labour," so the Jews' inquiry came in this verse:

6.10.1.en: "What shall we do?" as if their hearts had begun to incline, for a moment, to the spiritual teaching of the Lord Christ in doing the works of God, in order to obtain this food that endureth. Christ's answer to them was that all these works are summed up in faith in Him. And the Church teaches that faith in the Lord Jesus is the first condition of salvation, for spiritual striving and good works are accepted only on the basis of faith in the Redeemer Son whom the Father sent.

6.11.0.en: When Christ asked the Jews for faith in Him, they asked Him a direct question: "If the sign God gave to the prophet Moses in the time of our fathers was the coming down of manna from heaven, which is the greatest miracle and gift, because it sustained the whole people for 40 years, then what greater miracle do you work, that we may believe you, as our fathers believed Moses?"

6.12.0.en: Once again, as usual, the Lord tries to lift the Jews to what is higher and deeper, to bring them into the divine mysteries hidden from them, so He corrected the error: the manna was not Moses' gift to his people, but the gift of God the Father. And the Father Himself now gives them the greater and true bread, for the manna was a type of the true bread; Christ Himself, who came down from heaven incarnate, and the Giver of life to the world, is the true bread of life.

6.13.0.en: The Jews did not understand exactly Christ's intention, but they sensed the greatness of the gift and asked for it, imitating the Samaritan woman who asked for the living water without understanding the deeper meaning that Christ intended. For this reason Christ began, from (v. 35), the detailed explanation of the bread of life, which is above material gifts. We still, my God, ask for material things and are busy with them, while You call us to seek first the Kingdom of Heaven, and You would pour out on us every kind of gift. But we still stumble, and need Your strong arm to raise us and pull us out of what we are in, so that we care for what is above where You are, my God, and the soul is truly satisfied with being always with You, and does not turn back to ask for what is earthly.

6.14.0.en: The Lord Christ presents Himself as He presented Himself to the Samaritan woman: He is living water and the bread of life, that is, in Him are all of man's needs for life, and without Him there remain only the hunger and thirst which the world with all that is in it cannot make up for. And the phrase "I am" Christ used repeatedly: "I am the light of the world," "I am the door," "I am the way," "I am the truth," "I am the good shepherd," "I am the vine," "I am the resurrection," "I am the life." Likewise it affirms that He is the only One who fills all the needs of the human soul, however its demands or need may differ. Likewise the expression "never" corresponds to the expression "forever" in His discourse with the Samaritan woman. Christ's satisfaction is not limited to the variety of man's needs and his bodily, psychological and spiritual demands, but it is continuous, eternal satisfaction, that is, satisfaction without end.

6.14.1.en: As for man's responsibility in obtaining this satisfaction, the Lord Christ Himself defined it by His words: "he that cometh to me." So Christ offers and presents His gifts to man without imposing Himself; He stands and knocks at the door without opening it by force, so that man may have the will to choose, and this is a grave responsibility, for whoever does not come to Christ perishes of hunger and thirst, and remains in the torment of need for satisfaction without obtaining it ...

6.15.0.en: "Ye also have seen me, and believe not": that is, despite Christ's continued revelation of Himself in various ways, the eyes of the Jews remained in a state of spiritual blindness, because they did not seek the person of Christ for Himself, but because they ate of the loaves and were filled bodily (v. 26). So it is with man in all his conditions: if the basis of his relationship with God is only material benefit, God does not regard him as a believer, even if he claims to be.

6.15.1.en: "All that the Father giveth me": the Lord Christ attributed the act of giving and sending to the Father, and receiving and not rejecting to the Son, for the Son receives everyone who comes to Him, to obtain redemption first through faith in Him. The verse also bears the meaning of the acceptance of the Gentiles in this free redemption, for the Jews saw Him and did not believe. But whoever comes to Him He does not reject, and does not cast out. And how could He, when He is the Lover of mankind, the tender One, who in His love receives the whole world, being incarnate and crucified for us all. What a hope given to all sinners in His ever-open embrace. I thank You, my God, for Your words that encourage our weak souls ... whenever we come acknowledging and confessing our sins, and the priest reads to us the prayer of absolution, we remember Your true promise that whoever comes to You You will not cast out, but You establish him in Your love, and cleanse him that he may bring forth more fruit.

6.16.0.en: The speech here continues the meaning of the previous verses, for Christ affirms that the reason for His coming down from heaven, that is, His incarnation, is the fulfillment of the one will of God: the Father's will is the salvation of all, and the Son is the fulfiller of this will by His death and redemption. So of all that the Father has given to the Son, nothing is lost from it, but it is kept in the name of Christ for the day of His Second Coming, and the resurrection from the dead.

6.17.0.en: Christ continues to explain and clarify the will and purpose of the Father, which are, simply, faith in His only begotten Son, apart from whose name there is no other by which we can be saved (Acts 4:12). The following truths of the faith can be drawn out:

6.17.1.en: (1) That salvation is based on faith in Christ, and this condition was repeated by Christ Himself, and likewise by the Apostles, many times without concession. For this reason the Church believes that salvation is available to the whole world, but its first condition is faith in Christ. And because of this clarity in Christ's words, the Church rejects the heresy of universal salvation (that is, the salvation of people even without their faith in Christ).

6.17.2.en: (2) That faith, although it is the first condition, nevertheless has other matters without which faith is nullified, and the coming verses of the same chapter will deal with another condition for salvation. For this reason, when the Church interprets the Holy Bible, she does not rely on a single verse, but takes the meaning of the verses as a whole.

6.18.0.en: Christ's bodily circumstance, according to lineage, stood as a stumbling block before the Jews in accepting His divinity, and they did not accept what the Lord had repeated in 3 earlier verses, that He is the bread that came down from heaven (vv. 33, 35, 38). Their reaction was to murmur at Him, to make light of His words, and not to accept the idea of the Incarnation. "Jesus, the son of Joseph": this is what the Jews knew, in their bodily perception, of the person of Christ. And St. Luke was precise when he referred to this lineage in his Gospel, saying: "as was supposed" (Lk 3:23), that is, the common view and not the true one.

6.19.0.en: The Lord Christ explains here the inability of the human mind alone to have faith and to follow Christ, for the Father must draw man by the act of the divine gift of faith, and by teaching man through divine inspiration. And the expression the Lord used here: "They shall be all taught of God," is what came on the lips of the prophets (Isa 54:13; Jer 31:33-34), in clear references to the divine role in teaching man the mysteries of the faith, without which man cannot come to Christ.

6.20.0.en: No man has been able, is able, or will be able to see God, as God Himself said: "for there shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). But Christ, being "in the bosom of the Father" (ch. 1:18), and one with the Father (ch. 10:30), is the only eternal One who has seen the Father, and who can reveal Him to us. "Verily, verily, I say unto you": an expression the Lord used often to demonstrate the truth of what He teaches, which is that there is no eternal life, and no salvation, for anyone who does not believe in Christ, who is one with the Father in essence.

6.21.0.en: "I am the bread of life": Christ repeats what He declared in (v. 35), which the Jews did not understand, and they murmured at Him. This verse is regarded as an introduction to the divine mysteries that the Lord will declare concerning this bread. My beloved brother ... let us learn from the Lord Christ here the necessity of holding to the sound faith, for the Lord Christ was long-suffering, and went on explaining, and will complete His explanation, but He never yielded, under the weight of pressures or murmuring, from sound teaching. So has Your Church been throughout the ages, from the days of the pure Apostles, passing through Athanasius and Cyril and others who kept the faith pure and sound, exactly as Christ delivered it, without neglect or alteration ...

6.22.0.en: If manna was the greatest of the divine gifts in which Israel boasted, Christ makes clear here that it was only food to keep the body alive, whose end in any case is death. This verse is regarded as a comparison, and an introduction to a long discourse to come about the true living bread ...

6.23.0.en: The Lord Christ reveals to us here the greatest mysteries and gifts of the New Testament: that He is the bread that came down from heaven, in a clear reference to His incarnation, and in His being the source of life, so that whoever eats of it does not die. The manna of the Old Testament was therefore a type that gave life to the body. But Christ, the bread of life, whoever eats Him lives forever, because He is the food of the spirit, contrary to what the Jews wanted or understood. And the phrase "live for ever" means that bodily death cannot harm him. The summary of this is that Christ is the living God and the Giver of life, and He offers His body and blood as the bread of life, so whoever eats of this body and drinks of this blood is united with the One who bestows and gives life. How then shall he die? Rather, the death that is in us becomes life by our union with this heavenly bread. Do you understand now, dear one, the extent of the Church's concern for the sacrament of Holy Communion, and her constant call to all her children to partake of it, because it is eternal life ... it is union with Christ ... it is the forgiveness of sins.

6.24.s.en: (6) The efficacy of the body and blood of Christ

6.24.0.en: "The Jews therefore strove": that is, the Jews were divided between supporting and opposing what Christ had declared, that He is the bread of life, and His body given for the salvation of the world. This lack of understanding reminds us of both Nicodemus (ch. 3) and the Samaritan woman (ch. 4), in their failure to grasp the divine mysteries. And the expression "How can?!" also carries something of mockery at what Christ said.

6.25.0.en: Yet Christ answers them with what is harder, for it is not eating the flesh only, but drinking the blood also, and Christ's use of the expression "Son of man" is a reference to His incarnation and death; and by His death as a sacrifice He gives His body for the life of the world. And as the Passover lamb was a sacrifice whose eating was bound up with the salvation and deliverance of all the people of Israel, so the body of Christ given gives deliverance and salvation. As for the one who abstains from and rejects this living sacrifice, he is spiritually dead in this life, and likewise in the age to come.

6.25.1.en: So come, beloved, and enjoy the greatest of the divine gifts, and do not deprive yourself of life in Christ and through Christ, for you are the desire of His heart, and the object of His love; do not deprive yourself of Him, and do not make Him wait for you.

6.26.0.en: The sacrifice of Christ, His body and blood and salvation, has been granted to the whole world. But none will enjoy eternal life except one who eats of this sacrifice. Therefore, partaking of the body and blood of the Lord has become a condition for this salvation and eternal inheritance.

6.27.0.en: That is, not a symbol nor an image, but reality. This verse is the most eloquent of the verses answering all who claimed that the sacrifice of Christ in the sacrament of Holy Communion is nothing but a symbol or a remembrance, ignoring Christ's affirmation that His flesh is meat indeed and His blood is drink indeed. And we do not know what more they ask Christ to say than this, that they may believe?!

6.28.0.en: A new gift is given by partaking of the body and blood of Christ, which is the gift and bestowal of abiding. A branch that is cut off has no value and no life in it. But if the branch abides in its source there is fruit, and Christ Himself said: "without me ye can do nothing" (ch. 15:5). As the sap of life flows into the branches of the tree, so the blood of Christ in our bodies gives us abiding, connection and growth ...

6.29.0.en: My Father is the source of life and I am life itself (as if we were to say: the Father is the mind, and the Son is the thought). And I give spiritual eternal life to everyone who eats the sacrifice of My body.

6.30.0.en: The Lord Christ concludes His discourse here about His body and blood by returning to the beginning of the discourse (vv. 32, 33) in the comparison between the gift of food for the body, "manna," and the greater gift, namely His body given for the life of the world. This verse comes as a summary of all that was said, and a confirmation of what preceded in verses 33, (50, 51, 54, 57).

6.30.1.en: My beloved God ... we worship You in thanksgiving for the greatness of the riches of Your gifts which are above our minds and our understanding, and which none understands except one who was born of the Holy Spirit in Baptism, this which St. Gregory chanted in the Divine Liturgy: "You who have given me this service full of mystery ... You have given me the offering up of Your body in bread and wine."

6.30.2.en: We thank You, our God, because in Your body is eternal life (v. 51), the second resurrection (v. 54), abiding in You (v. 56), and union with You and the Father in respect of life (v. 57).

6.30.3.en: Grant us never to depart from the table of life, Your holy altar, where is the gift of Your most holy body.

6.31.0.en: St. John took care to mention that this whole discourse was in the synagogue, and by specifying the place at the end of the discourse he intended to declare that it was not a private discourse to the disciples, but a public proclamation of the truths of the faith, before the priests and all the people.

6.32.0.en: The disciples here do not mean the Twelve and the other seventy apostles, but the many who followed Him from place to place, considering themselves disciples of His ... And what made them stumble was two things: His saying that He is the bread of life that came down from above, and the emphasis on the necessity of eating His flesh and drinking His blood, for they understood His words literally. Jesus knew by His divinity that His words made them stumble, and He told them so.

6.33.0.en: If you do not accept what I have said now, how will it be with you when you see Me ascending to heaven, where I was before? For Christ, until now, had not solved for these people their first problem of eating His flesh and drinking His blood, but added to it a new problem, as He speaks of His eternity, referring to His ascension to the bosom of His Father, where He was before His incarnation (Mk 16:19; Lk 24:51; Acts 1:9).

6.34.0.en: The simple meaning of this verse is that Christ offers those who stumbled at His words the solution, which is that His words must be believed spiritually, apart from limited rational and material understanding: "they are spirit, and they are life." As for the meaning of "the flesh profiteth nothing," St. Augustine and St. Cyril the Great agreed that the meaning Christ intended is: if your conception is of eating My flesh in a material sense, as though you were eating material meat, it profits nothing for eternal life. But what profits is that you eat My true flesh united with My divinity. This is what He explained to His disciples afterward at the Last Supper on Holy Thursday, when He gave them His body and blood under the appearances of bread and wine. And this is the spiritual faith that gives eternal life. See the institution of the sacrament in (Mt 26:26, Mk 14:22, Lk 22:17, 19).

6.35.0.en: A strong reference to the divinity of the Son, in respect of foreknowledge, which belongs to God alone, for He knows that among those who hear Him are some who do not believe His words. And so that we may know that this was not Christ's inference from reading the faces of the crowd, St. John adds the words "from the beginning," to affirm this divine aspect of Christ's foreknowledge, also indicating that Christ's knowledge is not only of those who do not accept His words, but of the disciple who was about to betray Him as well.

6.36.0.en: Christ reminds them of what He said earlier in vv. 44, 45, that man cannot come or be received to Christ unless the faith which the Father has put in his heart is the true and only motive. But whoever comes from a utilitarian, or self-interested, or political motive, such as the liberation of the Jews, Christ will be a stumbling block to him; and this is what Simeon the elder said in his prophecy, that He is "set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel" (Lk 2:34).

6.37.0.en: That is, the people who rejected His saying that His flesh is meat indeed and His blood is drink indeed.

6.37.1.en: My beloved God, we lift to You a prayer whose subject is those who every day leave You and go back, and no longer walk with You ... They leave the living fountain of life, and leave the embrace of Your love, for what, my God ... for material things and cares, from which man reaps nothing but toil without rest ... My God ... do not allow us, the weak, to be distracted from You by anything, but let us remain with You in Your Church, taking of Your love and Your giving, serving Your holy name all the days of our life ... Amen.

6.38.0.en: It is not meant that Christ wanted to know their intention, He who knew from the beginning who would leave Him and who would follow Him, but the purpose of this question was to test their faith and their confession of Him. For this reason Peter's answer came fully in agreement with Christ's question, and it was also an expression of what was within the rest of the disciples, and it carries a strong faith. And the phrase "To whom shall we go?" means we have no one but You, and we cannot turn back as the others did. And the phrase "Thou hast the words of eternal life" is an affirmation of all that Christ said in the previous verses about eternal life, and that He is its source and giver, as the bread of life and the gift of His most holy body and blood.

6.39.0.en: Peter continues his speech, in declaring the disciples' position with Him, that the basis of their following Christ is the faith given to them by the Father, and it is a following that will continue regardless of those who left Him: our faith in You that You are the Christ the Savior, and that You are the Son of the living God, will leave us no other room to leave You, otherwise we would be as though leaving life for death, and eternity for destruction.

6.40.0.en: The Lord Christ completes the revelation of His divine knowledge by correcting Peter's words, saying to him:

6.40.1.en: You have spoken, Peter, for all your brother disciples with words of good faith, but this is not the confession of all as you said, for among you is one who does not believe, but Satan has filled his heart, and he is the one who will betray me and deliver me up ... And let us note here the Lord's saying: that despite my choosing you and your discipleship, among you is a devil. And this means that God chooses man and calls him, but man may abide or leave God by his free will. Consequently, the teaching that a believer never perishes is a strange teaching, for God also chose Judas, but Judas did not abide in this choice, so his was destruction.

6.40.2.en: Christ's discourse about Himself and the Holy Spirit; the faith of the crowd and the rejection of the leaders
